prompt: Match each delivery guarantee to what a crash costs under it.

pairs.right: a message that is never processed

prompt: A consumer acknowledges each message as soon as it receives it, then does the work. What does a crash during the work cost?

choices.text: The message is processed twice
choices.why: That is what acknowledging after the work risks.

choices.text: The message is lost, silently
choices.why: Right: at most once. Nobody will ever process it.

choices.text: The broker notices and redelivers it to another consumer after a timeout
choices.why: It was acknowledged, so the broker considers it done.

choices.text: Nothing, because the work is retried automatically
choices.why: Nothing retries work the broker thinks is finished.

prompt: A vendor says its broker delivers exactly once. Why does the lesson say that cannot cover your consumer's database?
hint: What can the broker not see?

choices.text: Brokers lose messages more often than they claim
choices.why: The argument is not about losses.

choices.text: Exactly once is forbidden by the AMQP protocol
choices.why: No protocol forbids it; the gap is between two systems.

choices.text: It cannot see inside your transaction
choices.why: Right. A crash between your commit and its acknowledgement leaves the two disagreeing.

choices.text: Databases do not support transactions across tables
choices.why: They do; the gap is between the database and the broker.

prompt: Acknowledging after the work, so that a crash repeats the work rather than losing it, gives at ___ once delivery.
In the lab, what stands in for the card processor?
hint: Where does a charge end up?

choices.text: The RabbitMQ queue `charges`
choices.why: That is where requests wait, not where they are charged.

choices.text: A row in the consumer's SQLite database
choices.why: Right, so a double charge can be counted.

choices.text: A call to a test API on the internet
choices.why: The lab makes no call outside the machine.

choices.text: The outbox table in the shop's database
choices.why: The outbox holds messages to send, not charges.

prompt: Why does every script call `connect()` from `topology.py` before doing anything?
hint: Lesson 6 lost two messages because of the order things ran in.

choices.text: So the layout exists whichever script runs first
choices.why: Right. A publish can never land on an exchange with no queue bound.

choices.text: Pika refuses to publish unless the queue was declared in the same process
choices.why: Pika publishes to exchanges; the reason is the layout, not the library.

choices.text: Declaring a queue twice deletes the messages in it
choices.why: Declaring an existing queue with the same settings changes nothing.

choices.text: It opens a separate connection for each queue
choices.why: It opens one connection and one channel.

prompt: After the naive consumer crashed and ran again, how many cents had been charged for order `q-1`, whose basket cost 3,290?
Why did RabbitMQ deliver `q-1` a second time?
hint: What did the broker never receive?

choices.text: The publisher sent it twice
choices.why: It was published once, and confirmed once.

choices.text: The charge failed the first time
choices.why: The first charge was committed; the list shows it.

choices.text: The acknowledgement never arrived
choices.why: Right. To the broker the message was never handled.

choices.text: The queue is configured to deliver every message twice
choices.why: Nothing in the topology does that.

prompt: A colleague proposes skipping every message whose `redelivered` flag is true. What goes wrong?
hint: When else is the flag set?

choices.text: Nothing; the flag means it was processed
choices.why: The flag means it was handed out before, not that the work happened.

choices.text: RabbitMQ refuses to deliver a message twice once a consumer skips it
choices.why: The broker has no such rule.

choices.text: Every message has the flag set, so nothing is processed
choices.why: First deliveries have it false, as the lab showed.

choices.text: A crash before the work also sets it, and skipping loses the payment
choices.why: Right. Only the consumer's own records can tell the two cases apart.

prompt: Which of these operations is idempotent?
hint: Twice has the same effect as once.

choices.text: Adding 3,290 to a customer's balance
choices.why: Twice adds 6,580.

choices.text: Setting a product's price to 3,290
choices.why: Right. The second time changes nothing.

choices.text: Taking one unit of coffee out of stock
choices.why: Twice takes two.

choices.text: Sending a confirmation e-mail
choices.why: Twice sends two e-mails.

prompt: What did the idempotent consumer do with the redelivered `q-2`?

choices.text: Charged it again and printed a warning
choices.why: The list shows `q-2` once.

choices.text: Rejected it to the dead-letter queue as a duplicate
choices.why: It acknowledged it; a duplicate is not a failure.

choices.text: Skipped the charge and acknowledged it
choices.why: Right. The insert into `processed` failed on the key.

choices.text: Left it unacknowledged, so it stayed in the queue
choices.why: It was acknowledged, so the queue was emptied.

prompt: A consumer writes the message id to `processed`, commits, then charges in a second transaction. What does a crash between the two cost?
hint: Which fact gets written without the other?

choices.text: A double charge, as with the naive consumer
choices.why: The id is recorded, so a redelivery is skipped.

choices.text: A payment marked done and never charged
choices.why: Right: at most once, just moved. Both must be one transaction.

choices.text: Nothing, since the id protects against every failure
choices.why: The id protects only if it commits with the effect.

choices.text: The message goes to the dead-letter queue
choices.why: A crash does not reject a message.

prompt: Why must `processed` eventually have old rows deleted, and what decides how old?
hint: How late can a duplicate arrive?

choices.text: SQLite cannot hold more than a million rows
choices.why: The concern is growth, not a hard limit.

choices.text: Old ids must be deleted daily so they can be reused
choices.why: Ids are not reused.

choices.text: It never needs deleting, because rows are small
choices.why: A row per message grows without end.

choices.text: It grows for ever; keep ids longer than a duplicate could arrive late
choices.why: Right, bounded by redelivery and by how far back anyone might replay.

prompt: Who creates an idempotency key, and when?
hint: It has to survive a failure the server may never have seen.

choices.text: The server, when the first attempt arrives
choices.why: The caller needs the key before it knows whether the server saw anything.

choices.text: The caller, fresh for every retry
choices.why: A fresh key per retry identifies nothing.

choices.text: The caller, once, before the first attempt
choices.why: Right, and it keeps it so that every retry sends the same.

choices.text: The broker, which assigns one to every message
choices.why: HTTP calls have no broker; the caller supplies the key.

prompt: Match what the server finds for a key to what it does.

pairs.right: does the work and stores key and response

pairs.left: a key stored with a response

right_distractors: charges the card again, more carefully

prompt: The checkout's connection drops after it sent a payment request and before the answer came. What makes a retry safe?
hint: A stable name for one intended effect.

choices.text: Waiting ten seconds before retrying
choices.why: Time does not tell the server it has seen this payment.

choices.text: Sending the same `Idempotency-Key` again
choices.why: Right. The server returns the stored answer if it charged.

choices.text: Asking the card's bank whether it was charged
choices.why: The bank is not the API being called, and it is too late for the shop.

choices.text: Retrying with a lower amount
choices.why: A different amount is a different payment.

prompt: What did `mandatory=True` change when `q-3` was published with the key `refunds`?

choices.text: The broker created a `refunds` queue for it
choices.why: Brokers do not create queues for publishers.

choices.text: The broker returned it, and the script knew
choices.why: Right, where lesson 6's orders were dropped in silence.

choices.text: The broker delivered it to `charges` instead
choices.why: It went to no queue at all.

choices.text: Nothing; the message was still dropped silently
choices.why: The script printed that it was returned.

prompt: What does a publisher confirm tell the publisher?

choices.text: That the consumer has processed the message
choices.why: Confirms are between publisher and broker only.

choices.text: That its own database committed the order
choices.why: The broker knows nothing about the publisher's database.

choices.text: That the broker has taken the message
choices.why: Right: stored in every queue it was routed to.

choices.text: That the message will be delivered exactly once
choices.why: Confirms say nothing about delivery to consumers.

prompt: The shop commits an order and then publishes its message, and crashes between the two. What is the result?

choices.text: A payment for an order that does not exist
choices.why: That is the other order of the two writes.

choices.text: An order nobody will ever charge
choices.why: Right. The message was never sent.

choices.text: Both are rolled back together
choices.why: No transaction covers the database and the broker.

choices.text: The broker sends the message when the shop restarts
choices.why: The broker never received it.

prompt: With the broker stopped, what happened to order `o-1` in the lab?

choices.text: The order was refused, because the broker was down
choices.why: The order was saved; only relaying failed.

choices.text: The order was saved and its message lost
choices.why: The message waited in the outbox and was sent later.

choices.text: Order and message saved; relayed once the broker was back
choices.why: Right, and the payments consumer charged it.

choices.text: The relay kept retrying in a loop until the broker came back
choices.why: The relay reported the failure and exited.

prompt: Why does a system with a transactional outbox still need an idempotent consumer?
hint: What if the relay crashes after the confirm?

choices.text: Because the outbox sends each message exactly once
choices.why: It does not; that is the point.

choices.text: Because the outbox loses messages when the broker is down
choices.why: The lab showed it keeps them.

choices.text: It does not; the outbox makes the consumer's job safe on its own
choices.why: The relay can still send a message twice.

choices.text: A relay crash after the confirm resends the message
choices.why: Right. The outbox gives at least once, and the consumer absorbs the repeat.

prompt: The table in the shop's own database, written in the same transaction as the order and read by a relay, is called the ___.
Which of these keeps all the events of one order in order, in Kafka?

choices.text: More partitions, so that events are spread evenly
choices.why: Spreading one order's events breaks their order.

choices.text: The order id as the message key
choices.why: Right: one order, one partition, one consumer.

choices.text: A random key per message
choices.why: Random keys scatter one order across partitions.

choices.text: More consumers in the group
choices.why: Consumers do not change where messages were written.

prompt: Which of these can deliver one order's events out of order? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Competing consumers on one queue
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: A message redelivered after a crash
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Events spread over several partitions
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: One consumer reading one partition
choices.why: That is the arrangement that keeps order.

prompt: A team cannot guarantee the order of `OrderPaid` and `OrderShipped`. What does the lesson suggest instead of fighting the transport?
hint: What if order did not matter?

choices.text: Wait a minute before applying each event
choices.why: A delay narrows the window; it does not close it.

choices.text: Carry a version, apply only newer ones
choices.why: Right. Then the order of arrival stops mattering.

choices.text: Use a single queue for the whole company
choices.why: One queue still has redeliveries and competing consumers.

choices.text: Merge the two events into one message type
choices.why: The events describe different moments; merging them loses one.

prompt: What is a poison message?

choices.text: A message from an attacker
choices.why: The name is about failing, not about intent.

choices.text: A message delivered twice
choices.why: That is a duplicate, handled by idempotency.

choices.text: One whose processing fails every time
choices.why: Right, such as a body that is not valid JSON.

choices.text: One that arrived out of order
choices.why: Out of order can be handled; poison cannot.

prompt: The database timed out while a consumer handled a message. Should the message go to the dead-letter queue?

choices.text: Yes; any failure belongs there
choices.why: Transient failures may succeed on a retry.

choices.text: No: retry it later, with a delay
choices.why: Right. The dead-letter queue is for failures that will never succeed.

choices.text: Yes, and the consumer should stop until a person looks
choices.why: One slow database does not need a person.

choices.text: No: acknowledge it and move on
choices.why: That loses the payment.

prompt: After the broken `q-4` was rejected, how many messages did `charges.dead` hold?
Put the steps of the transactional outbox in order, from the order being placed to the charge.
hint: One transaction first, the broker later.
items: The order and its outbox row commit in one transaction
The relay reads the unsent row
The relay publishes and the broker confirms

The idempotent consumer charges the order

prompt: Quitanda's refund consumer adds the refunded amount to the customer's store credit. Which change makes it safe under at least once?

choices.text: Acknowledge each message before adding the credit
choices.why: That loses refunds when the consumer crashes.

choices.text: Skip messages marked as redelivered
choices.why: That loses refunds whose first attempt crashed before the work.

choices.text: Record the message id with the change, in one transaction
choices.why: Right. A repeat fails on the key and adds nothing.

choices.text: Send refunds through Kafka instead of RabbitMQ
choices.why: Kafka is at least once too.
